# adjacent-field — wave A (brief A-A5)

Adaptive clinical trial design borrows from **sequential analysis** (1940s–1970s operations research via Wald, Armitage, Pocock), **Bayesian decision theory** (posterior-driven stopping rules), and **information theory** (optimal data collection). However, the regulatory concept is sharply constrained by mandatory pre-specification—adaptive means protocol amendments are written before the trial starts, not emergent. This creates several false friends.

**Sequential Analysis (Genuine Foundation).** Group-sequential testing and interim analysis derive directly from Wald's SPRT (1945) and Armitage's clinical translation (1975). Pocock (1977) and O'Brien–Fleming (1979) established frequentist methods; ~61% of published adaptive trials use O'Brien–Fleming boundaries. Regulatory bodies recognize this as the backbone. *False friend:* Ad hoc protocol amendments during a trial are NOT adaptive design—FDA guidance (2019) explicitly distinguishes prospectively planned modifications from post-hoc changes.

**Bayesian Methods.** Bayesian inference naturally supports interim analysis (fewer theoretical adjustments than frequentist) and utility functions encode trial costs and ethical gains. Yet Bayesian ≠ adaptive; many fixed-design Bayesian trials exist, and under certain conditions, frequentist group-sequential rules and Bayesian rules converge (BMC comparative studies 2019). *False friend:* Authors sometimes conflate Bayesian methods with adaptive designs; regulatory guidance separates them.

**Multi-Armed Bandits (Critical Divergence).** Thompson sampling (1933, originally for non-clinical optimization) appears in some adaptive designs for response-adaptive allocation. But bandits optimize cumulative reward *during* the experiment; clinical trials must preserve statistical validity (Type I/II error control) and pre-specify sample size—fundamentally incompatible objectives. Bandits treat arms as independent reward sources; clinical trial arms are correlated (same outcome measure, shared biology). Regulatory guidance (FDA 2019, pp. 11–13) distinguishes Thompson-sampling allocation from full adaptive designs. *False friend:* Vendor and media coverage often labels "Thompson sampling in trials" as "bandit approach," creating confusion—trials cannot adopt pure bandit stopping criteria without losing Type I error control.

**Quality Control & CUSUM Monitoring.** CUSUM (Page 1954) uses sequential accumulation logic similar to interim analysis, but QC detects *process drift* (e.g., manufacturing defect), not treatment effect inference. Quality monitoring in clinical trials is *data quality* checking (protocol fidelity, data entry), not statistical inference. These are distinct objectives and statistical frameworks. *False friend:* "Statistical quality monitoring" sometimes called "SPC applied to trials"; they are unrelated.

**Machine Learning & Reinforcement Learning (Incommensurable).** ML predicts and optimizes loss; clinical trials test hypotheses and control error rates. RL requires large training datasets; trials stop as soon as ethical evidence accumulates. Stopping criteria differ: ML stops at performance plateau, trials at pre-specified N or efficacy/futility thresholds. Generalization priority (ML) vs. causal inference in target population (trials) are orthogonal. Transparent pre-specification is regulatory mandate; deep RL opaqueness is antithetical to trial requirements. *False friend:* "AI-enabled trials" conflates ML-driven heterogeneity modeling (legitimate *within* adaptive designs) with adaptive trial design itself; media often misuses "adaptive learning" (ML term) to mean adaptive trials (regulatory term).

**Agile Software Development (Opposite Philosophy).** The **most significant false friend.** Agile emphasizes responsive pivots to emergent needs; adaptive clinical trials require prospective specification of all protocol modifications—opposite axioms. Agile ships features and patches bugs on demand; trials pre-register stopping rules and cannot adjust for patient safety reasons once unblinded. Regulatory (FDA, EMA) and statistical validity requirements make agile methodology incompatible with regulated adaptive trials. 78% of Phase II trials have protocol amendments (Bhansali 2022), but this reflects *unplanned* adjustments—not adaptive design. *False friend:* Superficial terminological similarity masks incompatible governance and statistical frameworks.

**Convergence on Pre-Specification.** All legitimate adaptive trial methods share one non-negotiable requirement: protocol amendments prospectively specified before unblinded interim analysis. This separates true adaptive design from ad hoc flexibility, vendor "agility," or machine-learning optimization. Statistical communities agree; regulatory bodies enforce it.
